item.title: FactChecking Trump’s Post-Election ‘60 Minutes’ Interview
item.dc:creator: Paul Cuno-Booth
item.description: In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections that saw Democrats retake control of both the House and Senate, President Donald Trump blamed Republicans’ poor showing on “bad messaging” of his second term [trimmed]
item.content:encoded:
In his first sit-down interview since the midterm elections that saw Democrats retake control of both the House and Senate, President Donald Trump blamed Republicans’ poor showing on “bad messaging” — essentially not properly conveying to American voters all of the accomplishments of his second term.

But in his recounting of events, Trump repeatedly twisted the facts on the economy, immigration, gasoline prices, sanctions on Russia, crime and the reasons for the dramatic rise in his net worth during his presidency.

  • Pressed on whether his business ventures posed a conflict of interest, Trump falsely claimed the dramatic increase in his net worth since being reelected was due to the stock market’s rise, and he made other false or misleading claims.
  • Trump said the stock market “lost almost 2,000 points because of the Democrats'” sweeping victories in the midterms. The stock market has been volatile in the days after the election, but the Dow Jones was a little higher at the close on Nov. 9 than it was on Election Day. The S&P 500 is down slightly, less than 0.3%.
  • The president said there are people on the “pretty far right that would like everybody taken out” — referring to the deportation of all immigrants in the country illegally, even if they haven’t broken the law otherwise. But deporting everyone has been Trump’s stated position for years.
  • Trump claimed that he “didn’t lift diesel sanctions” on Russia. But his administration issued a temporary license in October that exempted imports of Russian diesel fuel from sanctions.
  • Trump falsely claimed that he had brought gas below $2 per gallon in Iowa before the war with Iran.
  • Asked about Americans’ views on the economy, particularly concerns about inflation, Trump said that “we have historically good numbers” and pivoted to talking about the stock market. Some economic metrics are indeed historically good, such as the low unemployment rate. But inflation has gone up under Trump.
  • The president misrepresented the polls and final margin in the Ohio Senate race, in claiming he boosted Republican Sen. Jon Husted’s chances.
  • Trump appeared to inflate the decrease in total crime in Washington, D.C., and he wrongly said that “we haven’t had a murder in a long time” in the city.

The president’s interview with Ross Douthat of CBS News’ “60 Minutes” was conducted on Nov. 6, and aired two days later.

Business Ventures and Net Worth

In one lengthy exchange, Douthat pressed Trump on his net worth skyrocketing while in office and whether his business ventures represented conflicts of interest. Trump made several false or misleading statements in response.

Stock market gains: Douthat brought up a Forbes story estimating Trump’s net worth had increased by roughly $3 billion since his reelection in 2024. 

“Well, so did everyone,” Trump responded, telling Douthat he “should’ve had stock” when the journalist said “my net worth did not go up by $3 billion.” 

It’s true that the stock market is higher than when Trump took office in January 2025. But that’s not the main source of the increase in his net worth. 

The New York Times reported in June, based on Trump’s financial disclosure forms, that he made at least $2.2 billion that year. About $1.4 billion of that came from his family’s cryptocurrency ventures, and additional revenue came from deals licensing his name and other sources.

Trump’s investments in financial markets also increased in value, the Times reported, but that wasn’t the main reason his wealth shot up.

Presidential salary: Trump falsely asserted that he’s the only American president to forego his annual salary of $400,000 and donate it instead.

“I don’t take a salary,” he said, adding that “every other president took their salary.” At one point he said that was “supposedly” the case. “I don’t know if that’s right.”

He’s made this boast before, but it’s untrue. Presidents Herbert Hoover and John F. Kennedy, both of whom were independently wealthy, did the same, Thomas F. Schwartz, director of the Herbert Hoover Presidential Library, wrote in 2016. 

Comparison to past presidents: Historians have said Trump’s business entanglements are unprecedented. But in the “60 Minutes” interview, he claimed his situation is no different than what past presidents did.  

This came in response to Douthat pressing Trump on whether his stake in World Liberty Financial, a cryptocurrency company he co-owns with his sons, poses a conflict of interest. The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this year that a company linked to the government of the United Arab Emirates paid $500 million for a 49% stake in World Liberty Financial in January 2025. 

“Every president has not owned a cryptocurrency company,” Douthat said.

“Well, but — but they own something, whatever crypto was at the time, okay?” Trump said. “You know, there’s crypto and before that there was oil and the — and every president has had this problem.” 

Presidential historians told the New York Times, however, that no other president has launched new business ventures shortly before taking office and then continued to profit from them while leading the country. They noted that other modern presidents, by contrast, had sought to minimize potential conflicts of interest by selling off stakes in businesses or placing them under independent management.

A White House spokesperson told the Times that “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public.”

Obama-Netflix deal: In claiming that his predecessors also profited from business deals while in office, Trump said Barack Obama “got $100 million from Netflix … during his presidency.”

This is false. Barack and Michelle Obama signed a content-production deal with Netflix in 2018, more than a year after leaving the White House. (The value of the deal was not publicly announced; CNN, citing anonymous sources, reported it was a “high 8-figure deal.”)

Stock Market

Trump said the stock market has plummeted due to the Democratic victories in the midterms. The stock market has been volatile in the days after the election, but the Dow Jones was a little higher at the close on Nov. 9 than it was on Election Day. The S&P 500 is down slightly, less than 0.3%.

“The market lost almost 2,000 points because of the Democrats,” Trump said. “They got in. And the world said, ‘I don’t want to invest with these people’ because they look what happened in France, they look what happened in Italy and all over the world. And they say, ‘This is the same ideology.'”

Trump is referring to a steep drop in the stock market on the Thursday after the election. But he’s ignoring the gains on the day after the election. The market has also rebounded some since that big drop, though that largely came after “60 Minutes” conducted the interview.

The stock market has been on a bit of a roller coaster since Election Day. The day after the election, when it was clear Democrats had seized control of both the House and Senate, the Dow Jones Industrial Average — which tracks 30 of the nation’s largest companies — leapt up 3%. But then the next day, all those gains were lost, and then some, with a drop of 3.4%. Since then, the Dow Jones has risen some, and at the close of the market on Nov. 9 was about 1.2% higher than it was on Election Day.

The S&P 500, which is made up of 500 large-cap companies, followed a similarly bumpy path, gaining 1.6% the day after the election before losing 4.4% the following day. It has risen a bit since then, and closed the day on Nov. 9 less than 0.3% lower than where it was on Election Day.  

“The immediate post-election rally has run its course,” David Kelly, chief global strategist and head of the global market insights strategy team for J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said in a piece posted Nov. 9. “People are now focusing on the things they were concerned about beforehand, such as the financing of the AI buildout.”

“I wouldn’t make too much of the sell-off,” Kelly said. “This is a hangover from the big post-election rally.”

Trump also boasted about the stock market’s performance since taking office for a second term, and said it has outperformed past presidents.

“We’re doing numbers that have never been done before,” Trump said. “401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich. And for some reason — remember during rallies I’d say, ‘Please look at your 401(k) before you go to vote.'”

The stock market has done well under Trump. The S&P, with dividends, grew 17.78% last year. It is up 11.24% with dividends reinvested this year so far. But the performance under recent past presidents has hardly been “a disaster,” as Trump said.

The average yearly S&P 500 return, with dividends, under President Joe Biden was 15.34%. It was 16.65% during Trump’s first term, and 14.7% under President Barack Obama.

Deportation Policy

Trump said his deportation policy “might be too tough” and that he was open to discussing a bipartisan immigration bill that would grant many immigrants in the country illegally a pathway to citizenship. But he said there was a group on the “pretty far right that would like everybody taken out.”

While Trump described that as a “pretty far right” faction of the White House, Trump has on numerous occasions said his aim was to deport all immigrants living in the country illegally.

That was Trump’s policy when he ran for president the first time in 2016, saying during a Feb. 25, 2016, Republican debate, “We have at least 11 million people in this country that came in illegally. They will go out.” Trump reiterated that goal in remarks to reporters on June 22, 2019: “Everybody that came into the country illegally will be brought out of the country very legally.”

On Dec. 8, 2024, around a month after winning the presidency for the second time, Trump was asked by Kristen Welker of NBC’s “Meet the Press” whether he planned to deport everyone in the country illegally over the next four years.

“Well, I think you have to do it … you have rules, regulations, laws,” Trump said. “They came in illegally. You know the people that have been treated very unfairly are the people that have been on line for 10 years to come into the country.”

Trump has stuck by that plan since taking office for a second time.
